screens.title: IPFS & Decentralized Storage for DApps
screens.subtitle: Why decentralised storage is essential, how IPFS content addressing works, and how to reference CIDs from smart contracts.

narration.text: In this lesson we will make storage for DApps match the decentralization of the blockchain. Centralized file hosting creates single points of failure and censorship risk, and that undermines a DApp’s guarantees. IPFS solves this by addressing content by what it is rather than where it sits. When you add a file to IPFS it is chunked, hashed, and given a content identifier, a CID. That CID allows any peer on the network to verify and retrieve the exact bytes you asked for. You will learn how to add files with the IPFS command-line, how gateways let browsers access IPFS content, and why pinning services are necessary to keep content available even when your node goes offline. Finally, we’ll show how to store those CIDs in a Solidity contract so an NFT or DApp can point to immutable off-chain assets. By the end you’ll understand the full workflow from local file to on-chain reference, and you’ll know the common pitfalls like failing to pin or mixing location-based URLs with content addresses. Think about one asset in your DApp you don’t want to lose — that asset is what we’ll keep safe with IPFS.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use IPFS for decentralized, content-addressed storage and save only compact CIDs on-chain to combine immutability with efficiency.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll learn and why each skill matters

narration.text: These objectives guide the practical skills and understanding you will build. First, you will explain why centralized storage is a weak link for DApps. That matters because one offline server or an act of censorship can break your app or remove NFT artwork, undermining decentralization. Second, you will understand IPFS core principles: content addressing and CIDs. Knowing this helps you verify file integrity and relies on cryptographic hashes rather than location URLs. Third, you will learn how to use the IPFS command-line to add and retrieve files, so you can move real assets onto the network and verify the generated CID. Fourth, you will integrate IPFS hashes into smart contracts as compact references, which keeps on-chain storage minimal while preserving immutability. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a clear practical step so you can both reason about and implement decentralized storage correctly. As you progress, watch for the common pitfall of assuming uploaded content stays available without pinning, and keep these objectives in mind as checkpoints for competency.

screens.subtitle: Hands-on commands and operational knowledge to keep content available

narration.text: Beyond concepts, you will gain operational skills that prevent common failure modes. First, learn what pinning is and why it matters: pinning tells nodes to retain content so it is not garbage collected when nodes free space. Second, become familiar with IPFS gateways and when they are useful to serve content to traditional browsers. Third, practice integrating the CID you receive from IPFS into a Solidity contract as a stable reference for metadata or images. Fourth, be able to diagnose lost content — you will check whether content was pinned and whether the CID format is correct. These skills are practical and durable: they reduce the chance your DApp becomes unreachable, they allow you to keep on-chain storage small, and they help you choose an appropriate pinning strategy. Each objective links a technical operation to the real-world effect it produces, so you can design systems that stay available and verifiable for users.

screens.title: Why centralized storage breaks decentralization
screens.subtitle: Single points of failure, censorship risk, and the consequences for DApps

narration.text: When you build a DApp, decentralization is more than just smart contracts. If static assets like your frontend, images, or NFT metadata live on a single web server, that server becomes a central point of failure. Servers can go offline, be legally compelled to remove files, or be changed by an operator. For an NFT collection this can mean the artwork disappears or is swapped, which destroys the trust that ownership implies. The practical consequence is a “rug pull” of metadata rather than funds. The definition you should hold is simple: decentralized storage removes reliance on a single host so content remains accessible and verifiable even if individual hosts fail. A real example: hosting a DApp UI on a single provider risks downtime that stops users from connecting to your contract, whereas hosting the same build on IPFS with pinned nodes preserves availability. A common misconception is that putting a URL in a smart contract makes the content immutable; it does not. A location URL points to whatever the host serves, so the bytes can change without changing the link. The takeaway: prefer content-addressed storage for assets that require integrity and permanence, and treat centralized hosting only as a temporary or mirrored backup. Ask yourself now: which assets in your project must survive provider changes?

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Centralized hosting introduces failure and censorship risks; critical DApp assets should use decentralized, verifiable storage.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why centralized storage breaks decentralization

Centralized hosts create single points of failure and enable content changes without cryptographic verification. That undermines a DApp's guarantees.

Definition
Centralized storage serves content by location. If the host removes or alters files, references in contracts can no longer guarantee the original content.
Common mistake
Putting a provider URL in a smart contract and assuming immutability. Location-based URLs can change.
Pro tip
Classify assets: which must be immutable? Those should be content-addressed and pinned.
Analogy

Think of a URL-based file as a rented billboard: the landlord can repaint it. A content-addressed CID is like an archival print stored in multiple libraries — the content is verifiable and immutable.

Scenario
If your NFT metadata points to https colon slash slash my-server dot com slash art one dot png, the server owner can replace that file. If the token instead stores a CID, any auditor can fetch and verify the exact bytes associated with ownership.
Key Takeaway

Design assets that require permanence using content-addressed storage rather than single-host URLs.

screens.title: IPFS fundamentals: content addressing and CIDs
screens.subtitle: How files are chunked, hashed, and identified on the network

narration.text: IPFS is a peer-to-peer protocol that stores and shares files by their content, not by location. The key mechanism is content addressing: files are split into chunks, each chunk is cryptographically hashed, and the collection produces a Content Identifier, or CID. That CID is unique to the exact bytes of the content, so any modification—even a single byte—changes the CID. This gives you immutability and tamper-evidence: anyone retrieving a CID can verify the data matches the identifier. Concretely, when you add a file to your local IPFS node, the node breaks it into chunks, computes hashes, and returns a CID you can use to fetch the file from any peer that has it. A practical example is adding an image for an NFT: you add the file, record the CID, and then store that CID in the token’s metadata. A common misconception is to treat the CID like a URL; the CID is not a location but a fingerprint. If content is available from multiple peers, retrieval succeeds regardless of which peer serves it, as long as at least one peer has been pinned or otherwise retains the data. The takeaway is to treat CIDs as the canonical, verifiable identity of content for your DApp.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A CID is a cryptographic fingerprint; it guarantees that retrieved content matches exactly what was added to IPFS.

content.html:
Definition

Content addressing and CIDs

Files are split into chunks and hashed. The resulting cryptographic identifier is a CID that names content by its bytes, not by where it lives.

How it works
  • Chunk the file into blocks.
  • Hash each block to produce deterministic identifiers.
  • Combine hashes into a root CID representing the whole file.
Why it matters
A CID lets anyone verify data integrity and retrieve the exact content regardless of which node serves it.
Misconception
A CID is not a server address. It does not tell you where the bytes are stored; it tells you which bytes you want.
Concrete example
Imagine you add an image used by an NFT. IPFS returns a CID. If someone later requests that CID, IPFS retrieves the exact image bytes from any node that has them and verifies the hash matches the CID.
Key Takeaway
Use CIDs as immutable references to ensure asset integrity across peers and time.
Check
If you change the file, expect a new CID. Always update the on-chain reference when content changes.
Mnemonic
CID = Content ID, like a fingerprint for the file.

screens.title: Adding and retrieving files with the IPFS CLI
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step workflow from local file to CID and retrieval

narration.text: The basic IPFS workflow is practical and repeatable. First, initialize a node and start the daemon; this creates a local peer that can add and retrieve content. Next, add your file or folder to IPFS using the add operation; the node will chunk and hash the content and then return one or more CIDs, including a root CID for folders. For example, adding a DApp build folder returns a root CID that represents the directory structure. Third, you can fetch content using the CID either through a public gateway or directly from peers on the network. If you use a gateway, a browser can open the content via an HTTP URL built around the CID. Fourth, verify availability by requesting the CID from another machine or by using the cat command to stream the bytes back to your terminal. A concrete example is adding an index. html and style. css, getting a root CID, and loading index. html through a gateway to validate the site renders. A common mistake is to assume the content will persist after the local node shuts down; unless another node pins it, the data can be garbage collected. The key takeaway is to practice the add and cat commands until you can move a small build into IPFS and confirm the returned CID resolves and matches your files.

keyIdea.title: Practical workflow
keyIdea.text: Initialize a node, add files to produce CIDs, retrieve via gateway or peer, and verify content with the cat command.

content.html:
Process Flow

IPFS CLI workflow

Follow these repeatable steps to move files into IPFS and confirm retrieval.

1 Initialize & run node
Create a local node and start the daemon so it can add and serve content on the network.
2 Add files
Use the add command to produce a CID for a file or root CID for a folder containing your build.
3 Retrieve & verify
Use a gateway or the cat command to fetch the bytes and confirm the CID matches the file.
4 Persist via pinning
If you need long-term availability, pin the content on one or more nodes or use a pinning service.
Concrete example
Add a small site folder, note the root CID, open index.html through a gateway to confirm rendering, then cat the file to verify bytes match your source.
Check your understanding
  • Why might a gateway stop serving your CID?
  • What does the cat command prove about a file?
Key Takeaway

Practice adding, retrieving, and verifying CIDs locally before integrating them into contracts to ensure the workflow is reliable.

screens.title: Gateways vs direct peer retrieval
screens.subtitle: When to use a gateway and when to rely on the IPFS network

narration.text: There are two common ways to access IPFS content: through a gateway or directly from peers. A gateway is an HTTP server that translates traditional browser requests into IPFS retrievals. It is convenient because it allows standard browsers to access content with an HTTP URL built around the CID. This is useful for quick demos or compatibility, but a gateway is still a centralized pathway and may be subject to the same availability issues as other servers if it stops caching or is restricted. Direct peer retrieval uses the IPFS protocol to find any node that has the content and request it from them. This is more decentralized but requires running an IPFS node or relying on peers. A practical scenario: for broad user access to a DApp UI, you might serve a pinned site through an established gateway for initial discovery, while expecting direct peer retrieval from users with IPFS-enabled clients. A common misconception is that using a gateway removes the need to pin; it does not. Gateways can fetch content from the network, but if no nodes persist the content, a gateway eventually cannot serve it. The takeaway is to choose gateways for compatibility and pinning for guaranteed persistence, and to design your deployment accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use gateways for compatibility and discovery; rely on pinned nodes and direct peers for true persistence and decentralization.

content.html:
Comparison

Gateways vs direct peers

Gateway
An HTTP bridge for browsers. Easy to use, broadly compatible, but can be a single point of failure if the gateway stops serving content.
Direct peer retrieval
Uses the IPFS protocol to find peers with the bytes. More decentralized and resilient when multiple nodes host the data.
Concrete scenario
You can publish a DApp CID and test it via a gateway to confirm rendering. For production resilience, ensure multiple nodes pin the CID so direct retrieval succeeds even if a gateway becomes unavailable.
Checklist
  • Do you need browser compatibility? Use a gateway for discovery.
  • Do you need permanence? Pin to multiple nodes or use a pinning service.
  • Are you avoiding central points? Encourage direct peer retrieval from users who run nodes.
Misconception
A gateway makes a CID persistent. In reality it only serves while the content exists somewhere on the network or the gateway caches it.
Key Takeaway

Plan for both compatibility and persistence: gateways for access, pinning for durability.

screens.title: Pinning and pinning services
screens.subtitle: Ensuring your content remains available on IPFS

narration.text: Pinning is the explicit act of telling an IPFS node to retain content so it is not eligible for garbage collection. When you add content locally it may be stored, but if your node goes offline and no one else retains that content, the network can lose it. Pinning services solve this by hosting your content on multiple nodes and keeping it pinned so availability persists. The chapter mentions pinning services like Pinata, Web3. storage, and Infura IPFS as examples of providers that ensure your content remains discoverable. In practice you would add your site or asset to a pinning service after receiving the CID and they will host copies. A common error is to assume pinning is unnecessary when you expect some peers to cache content; caches are transient. A practical example: after you add your DApp build folder and get a root CID, use a pinning service to pin that root CID across durable nodes so your front end stays available even when your machine is offline. The takeaway is simple: if the content matters to your users or contracts, pin it. Treat pinning as part of deployment for production DApps to avoid losing assets.

keyIdea.title: Persistence rule
keyIdea.text: Pin content you must keep; pinning services provide durable, multi-node hosting to prevent garbage collection.

content.html:
Definition

Pinning & pinning services

Pinning instructs nodes to keep specific CIDs indefinitely. Pinning services host pinned content across multiple nodes so your data remains available.

How to use
After you receive a CID, submit it to a pinning service to ensure it is stored by reliable nodes that remain online.
Examples
Pinning services maintain copies of your content so the CID resolves even if your original node is offline.
Concrete workflow
Add a build directory, receive a root CID, then use a pinning service to pin that root CID. Confirm the service reports the CID as pinned.
Why it matters
Without pinning, content can be garbage collected and cease to exist on the network, even if you previously published it.
Common mistake
Relying on a single personal node to keep content alive for production use. Use a pinning service for reliability.

screens.title: Storing CIDs in Solidity
screens.subtitle: Pattern for mapping tokens to CIDs and constructing token URIs

narration.text: Smart contracts should store only compact references such as CIDs rather than bulky assets. The chapter shows a minimal NFTMetadataStore contract pattern: a mapping from token ID to a string that contains the CID, a setter to assign a CID for a token, and a tokenURI function that returns a constructed resource locator combining the content scheme and the CID. This approach keeps the blockchain small and immutable: the contract records which CID applies to which token, and the actual metadata and image remain off-chain on IPFS. A concrete example: after you add an NFT metadata file to IPFS and receive its CID, a deploy script can call setTokenCID with the token ID and that CID. Later, tokenURI will produce a pointer that clients can resolve to fetch metadata. A common misconception is trying to store large blobs on-chain; that is prohibitively expensive and unnecessary when you can store only the CID. Also be careful with CID formats; store them consistently and ensure your client or gateway constructs the full access path reliably. The takeaway is to treat the smart contract as the verified index of immutable CIDs and keep actual asset hosting on IPFS with proper pinning.

keyIdea.title: Design principle
keyIdea.text: Store only the CID in the contract; construct token URIs off-chain from that CID so assets remain immutable and storage-efficient.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Store CIDs in a contract

Keep on-chain state compact by mapping token identifiers to their IPFS CIDs and returning a constructed URI when clients ask for metadata.

Pattern
  • Use mapping from uint to string for CID storage.
  • Provide a setter restricted in real contracts to minters or owners.
  • Compose a token URI by combining a scheme and the stored CID to point to metadata.
Example snippet (visual only)
// minimal conceptual layout
mapping(uint256 => string) private _tokenCIDs;
function setTokenCID(uint256 tokenId, string memory cid) public { _tokenCIDs[tokenId] = cid; }
function tokenURI(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (string memory) { string memory base = "ipfs://"; string memory cid = _tokenCIDs[tokenId]; return string(abi.encodePacked(base, cid, "/metadata.json")); }
Misconception
Saving large JSON or images on-chain rather than CIDs is costly and unnecessary; keep content off-chain and verifiable by CID.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: publish a DApp frontend to IPFS
screens.subtitle: Create a simple build, add it to IPFS, obtain the root CID, and confirm accessibility

narration.text: This walkthrough turns the theory into a hands-on practice you can repeat. Begin by initializing and running a local IPFS node so it can add and serve files. Next, create a small frontend build consisting of an index file and a stylesheet. Add the build folder recursively to IPFS; the add operation returns a root CID representing the directory. Copy that root CID and open it through a gateway to validate that index. html renders. If the file displays, the CID maps to the correct bytes. Then pin the root CID using a pinning service to make the site persistent beyond your local node. Finally, use the CID in your deployment script to call a contract setter that records the CID for a sample token. A common pitfall is forgetting to add the folder recursively or pin the root CID, which can produce a CID that looks correct but disappears when your node goes offline. The key learning is to practice the full loop: add files, verify rendering, pin for persistence, and store the CID on-chain. After completing these steps, reflect on whether you could reproduce the site from a different machine using only the CID.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Move a small frontend into IPFS, confirm the root CID resolves, pin it for persistence, and register the CID in a smart contract.

content.html:
Hands-on

Lab: publish a DApp frontend

Follow these checkpoints to publish and verify a simple DApp build on IPFS.

Checkpoint 1
Install and run a local IPFS node. Initialize and start the daemon so you can add content.
Checkpoint 2
Create index.html and style.css in a folder, then add the folder recursively to IPFS to obtain the root CID.
Checkpoint 3
Open the CID through a gateway and verify the page renders correctly.
Checkpoint 4
Pin the root CID with a pinning service to guarantee persistence beyond your local node.
Checkpoint 5
Use the CID in a deployment script to set the token CID in your contract so tokenURI resolves to your pinned metadata.
Example files
index.html and style.css form the build. Adding them recursively yields a root CID for the folder that points to index.html under that CID.
Common pitfall
Not adding the folder recursively or failing to pin the root CID causes missing files later.
Key Takeaway

Practice the full add-verify-pin-store loop to ensure your DApp assets remain available and verifiable.

screens.title: Integrating the CID with deployment scripts
screens.subtitle: How to record a CID in a contract after publishing assets

narration.text: After you have a pinned CID, integrate it into your deployment pipeline. The typical flow is: publish your assets to IPFS, capture the returned root CID, and then call a setter on your deployed contract to associate that CID with a token or a collection. In practice you write a short interaction script that calls the contract's setTokenCID function with the token identifier and the CID string. Doing this from a deployment environment ensures the on-chain state references the exact content you published. A concrete example: deploy the NFTMetadataStore contract, then run a script that calls setTokenCID for token one with the root CID you pinned. Afterwards, call tokenURI for token one to confirm the constructed URI points to the metadata stored on IPFS. A frequent mistake is pasting an incorrectly formatted CID or forgetting to pin the metadata's CID rather than just pinning assets; always pin the metadata file if the contract points to it. The essential lesson is to automate the handoff from publishing to contract recording so the on-chain reference is always the CID returned by a verified add operation.

keyIdea.title: Deployment rule
keyIdea.text: After publishing, immediately pin and record the exact CID on-chain using an automated script to avoid mismatches and availability issues.

content.html:
Process

From CID to on-chain reference

Automate publishing, pinning, and recording the CID so your contract always points to a verified asset.

Step
Publish files, capture the root CID, pin it, and then call the contract setter with that exact CID string.
Example check
After storing the CID, call tokenURI and resolve the returned pointer to confirm metadata loads from IPFS as expected.
Script snippet (visual)
// deploy contract, then interact to setCID
// call setTokenCID(1, 'YOUR_ROOT_CID') and then tokenURI(1) to verify
Pitfall
Recording a CID before pinning can lead to an on-chain pointer that later resolves to nothing if the CID gets garbage collected.
Key Takeaway

Automate the chain: publish, pin, then record the exact CID to guarantee the contract points to persistent content.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Why content becomes unavailable and how to diagnose it

narration.text: Several common errors cause content to become unavailable on IPFS. The most frequent is not pinning content: adding files locally without pinning ensures data exists only while your node is online. If the node goes offline and no other node has pinned the CID, the content can be garbage collected and lost. Another mistake is storing location-based URLs in contracts instead of CIDs; the file can change or disappear without the contract reflecting that change. Incorrect CID formats or truncations also prevent resolution — store CIDs exactly as returned by the add operation. To troubleshoot, first verify the CID string is complete and correct. Then check whether the CID is pinned by your node or by a pinning service. If you cannot fetch via a gateway, try the cat command locally and confirm the bytes match your original file. A helpful diagnostic step is to attempt retrieval from a different machine or node to determine whether the issue is local. The takeaway is to treat availability as an operational requirement: pin critical content and verify resolution from multiple locations after publishing.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: If a CID stops resolving, check CID correctness, pin status, and whether other nodes host the content; retrieve from multiple locations to isolate the failure.

content.html:
Pitfalls

Common mistakes and troubleshooting

Not pinning
If only your local node hosts the content, it can be garbage collected when nodes free space. Use pinning services for production assets.
Wrong CID format
A truncated or mistyped CID will fail resolution. Always use the exact string returned by the add operation.
Diagnostic step
Try retrieving the CID from another node and use the cat command to confirm the bytes. If retrieval fails across nodes, the CID likely wasn't pinned anywhere.
Checklist
  • Is the CID exactly as returned when you added the file?
  • Is the CID pinned on one or more nodes?
  • Can you cat the file locally and does it match the source?
Key Takeaway

Treat persistence as part of deployment. Pin critical assets and confirm resolution from multiple peers to avoid surprises.

screens.title: Assessment idea: reasoning about decentralization and IPFS
screens.subtitle: Two practical questions to test your understanding

narration.text: Use these assessment questions to check your grasp of the material and to practice explaining the concepts. First question: why is storing NFT artwork on a centralized server and putting that URL in a contract a bad practice? An effective answer explains single points of failure, censorship risk, and the possibility of content changes that break immutability. It should also connect to IPFS as a solution: content addressing with a CID makes the reference verifiable and prevents silent changes. Second question: if the CID that pointed to your DApp stops resolving after several weeks, what likely happened and how would you fix it? The correct response names garbage collection due to no pinning, recommends using a pinning service or pinning on multiple nodes, and suggests verifying the exact CID and whether it was pinned. When you answer, include a short troubleshooting plan: verify CID integrity, try retrieval from another node, check pin status, and repin from your original source if necessary. These questions train you to reason both conceptually and operationally about content availability. Assessment idea: reasoning about decentralization and IPFS means explain why location-based urls are brittle, and demonstrate steps to diagnose and restore an unavailable cid.. In practical terms, two practical questions to test your understanding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assessment focus
keyIdea.text: Explain why location-based URLs are brittle, and demonstrate steps to diagnose and restore an unavailable CID.

content.html:
Assessment

Practice questions

Question 1
Explain why using a centralized URL in a smart contract threatens immutability and how IPFS/CIDs address that risk.
Question 2
Your DApp CID no longer resolves after weeks. Outline the most likely cause and a step-by-step repair plan.
Rubric hints
  • Mention single point of failure and mutable hosts for Q1.
  • Mention garbage collection and pinning for Q2.
  • Include verification steps like cat and cross-node retrieval.
Reflection prompt
Which asset in your project would cause the most damage if lost, and how would you protect it using IPFS and pinning?
Key Takeaway

Use assessments to rehearse both the conceptual justification for IPFS and the operational steps for keeping content available.

narration.text: These are the concepts to carry forward. Decentralized storage avoids single points of failure and censorship. IPFS is a peer-to-peer protocol that stores and shares data using content addressing. Content addressing means files are identified by cryptographic hashes instead of location. CIDs are those unique content identifiers and guarantee the content's integrity. Pinning instructs nodes to retain content so it is not garbage collected. Gateways let browsers access IPFS content via HTTP but do not replace the need to pin. Hold these definitions in mind as concise tools: when in doubt about permanence, pin; when in doubt about integrity, use CIDs. These short definitions will help you explain choices to teammates and design resilient DApp deployments. Key Concepts — What to Remember means cids = fingerprints, pinning = long-term holding, gateways = compatibility bridge.. In practical terms, core terms and one-line meanings. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory aid
keyIdea.text: CIDs = fingerprints, pinning = long-term holding, gateways = compatibility bridge.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick reference
screens.subtitle: Three short cards to lock in memory

narration.text: These final three concept reminders close the lesson. CID: the unique cryptographic identifier for content on IPFS; it ensures integrity because any change to bytes yields a different CID. Pinning: the act of instructing nodes to retain content forever, which is how you guarantee availability beyond your local node. IPFS Gateway: an HTTP bridge that translates browser requests into IPFS retrievals, useful for compatibility but not a substitute for pinning. Keep these three in mind when designing DApp deployments: identify assets to pin, rely on CIDs for verifiability, and use gateways for accessibility while preserving decentralization with pinned nodes. Key Concepts — Quick reference means cid for integrity, pinning for persistence, gateway for access — combine all three for resilient dapps.. In practical terms, three short cards to lock in memory. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Key Concepts
CID (Content Identifier)
A cryptographic fingerprint that names content and guarantees integrity.
Pinning
Tell nodes to retain a CID so the content is preserved and not garbage collected.
IPFS Gateway
An HTTP bridge for browser access; useful but not a replacement for pinning.
Final takeaway

Treat CIDs as authoritative, pin important content for persistence, and use gateways for compatibility while maintaining decentralization.

Access the content via `ipfs.io/ipfs/<CID>`. Next, show the Solidity `NFTMetadataStore` contract and explain how CIDs are stored.
